intro: You play a 16-year-old who loves maths and football and has to rebuild her life in a new country. Much of the way is paperwork and waiting that nobody asked her to carry. Her languages, her team spirit and the people who open doors count for a lot.

office.why: Papers and recognition: foreign diplomas and residence status are decided slowly, whatever your effort.

tunnel.why: Arriving without the language: for a while you understand little, and few people understand you.

ladder.why: School tracks: pupils with a migrant background more often land on lower tracks at equal marks.

sprint.why: Sport club: football needs no shared language, and clubs are a common first home for refugee children.

bridge.why: Teachers, neighbours and volunteers open doors for newly arrived families.

advantage.title: A helping hand
advantage.text: Neighbours, a teacher and a language buddy opened doors for Amira in a new country. After rolling, add 2 to your result.

life.title: Home (fictional)
life.text: Amira is an invented character, based on what many refugees report. She is 16, loves maths and football. Her father teaches, her mother is a nurse. Then war reaches her city and damages the school and the hospital.

life.title: Leaving everything
life.text: Her family decides to leave. They can only take what they can carry. Amira says goodbye to friends, her grandmother and her school books.

life.title: Months on the road
life.text: The journey takes months and depends on strangers, closed borders and long waits. Amira keeps her little brother calm by telling him stories.

life.title: Kindness at a border camp
life.text: A volunteer doctor treats her brother. A teacher gives Amira a notebook, so she can keep doing maths. Small acts of help carry a family a long way.

life.title: Arrival in Germany
life.text: The family lives in a shared accommodation and waits for months for papers and a school place. Everything is new: the language, the food, the rules, the weather.

life.title: Why can't her parents work?
life.text: In Germany her father drives a delivery van. Her mother cannot work as a nurse. Why?

q.q: Why can Amira's parents not work as a teacher and a nurse?
a: Their foreign qualifications are not recognised yet
They do not want to work
Refugees are never allowed to work
q.x: Recognising foreign diplomas is slow and complicated in many countries. The skills are there, the system is the barrier.

life.title: A language she doesn't speak yet
life.text: In class Amira understands little. She is quick at home, but here some classmates see only a girl who cannot speak. A few tease her scarf.

life.title: A teacher and Jana
life.text: A teacher stays after class to practise German with her. A classmate, Jana, invites her to football. Amira starts to feel she belongs somewhere.

life.title: Waiting for a decision
life.text: The family waits years for a decision on their status. Plans for study, work and travel stay on hold, because the rules decide, not effort.

life.title: Which school track?
life.text: A counsellor suggests a shorter, practical path. Amira wants to study medicine. Studies look at this pattern.

q.q: What do studies find about pupils from migrant families with the same grades?
a: They are more often advised to take lower school tracks
They are always advised to take the highest track
Their track advice is identical to everyone else's
q.x: Research on school recommendations in Germany shows a bias against migrant families. Mentors and teachers can help push back.

life.title: Her Abitur
life.text: With extra tutoring and a mentor, Amira insists on the Abitur and passes it. Her parents are proud, and she is accepted to study medicine.

life.title: Interpreting at the clinic
life.text: Amira volunteers as an interpreter for new arrivals. She knows how it feels to have nobody who understands you. She now feels at home in two places.

sources: OECD: Education in Germany, students with a migrant background
flags: The track-advice quiz states a widely reported finding about Germany; check the exact wording against an OECD/IQB source.

evidence.ev: Refugees in Germany often wait months or years for residence decisions, and foreign diplomas have to pass a recognition procedure before they count.
Newly arrived pupils often sit in class before they speak German; this isolates them even when they are strong in maths or sport.
At the same performance level, pupils with a migrant background are placed in lower school tracks more often (OECD, German school studies).
Sports clubs are one of the most common first places where refugee children find friends; the DOSB has run integration programmes since 1989.
Teachers, volunteers and neighbours are one of the most important factors for refugee children arriving in a new country (UNHCR).
